section.title: The Triumphal Entry
section.sectionRationale: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the promised King, humble on a donkey, to shouts of Hosanna. He acts with royal and prophetic authority in the temple, cleansing it and receiving the praise of children, and He curses a barren fig tree as an enacted parable of fruitless religion.
section.thesis: The gentle King foretold by the prophets comes to His city and His temple to claim them, purging the house of prayer, welcoming the praise of the least, and pronouncing judgment on fruitless, leafy religion that has no fruit for God.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the King's humble entry to Hosannas; the cleansing of the temple and the children's praise; and the withered fig tree with the lesson on believing prayer.

verses.text: As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent out two disciples,
saying to them, “Go into the village ahead of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied there, with her colt beside her. Untie them and bring them to Me.
If anyone questions you, tell him that the Lord needs them, and he will send them right away.”
This took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet:
“Say to the Daughter of Zion, ‘See, your King comes to you, {{praus|gentle}} and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’”
So the disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them.
They brought the donkey and the colt and laid their cloaks on them, and Jesus sat on them.
A massive crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.
The crowds that went ahead of Him and those that followed were shouting: “{{hosanna|Hosanna}} to the Son of David!” “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest!”
When Jesus had entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred and asked, “Who is this?”
The crowds replied, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.”

units.label: Jesus cleanses the temple
units.note: a house of prayer, not a den of robbers

verses.text: Then Jesus entered the temple courts and drove out all who were buying and selling there. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves.
And He declared to them, “It is written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer.’ But you are making it ‘a den of robbers.’”
The blind and the lame came to Him at the temple, and He healed them.
But the chief priests and scribes were indignant when they saw the wonders He performed and the children shouting in the temple courts, “Hosanna to the Son of David!”
“Do You hear what these children are saying?” they asked. “Yes,” Jesus answered. “Have you never read: ‘From the mouths of children and infants You have ordained praise’?”
Then He left them and went out of the city to Bethany, where He spent the night.
In the morning, as Jesus was returning to the city, He was hungry.
Seeing a fig tree by the road, He went up to it but found nothing on it except leaves. “May you never bear fruit again!” He said. And immediately the tree withered.
When the disciples saw this, they marveled and asked, “How did the fig tree wither so quickly?”

“Truly I tell you,” Jesus replied, “if you have {{pistis|faith}} and do not doubt, not only will you do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen.
If you believe, you will receive whatever you ask for in prayer.”

praus.gloss: Gentle, meek, humble. Matthew's word for the King of Zechariah's prophecy: this King comes not on a warhorse but gentle, on a donkey, strength under control, the same meekness Jesus blesses in the Beatitudes and claims of Himself, come to Me for I am gentle and lowly.

hosanna.gloss: A transliterated Hebrew cry from Psalm 118:25, meaning save now or save, we pray. Once a plea for deliverance, it had become a shout of praise; the crowds hail Jesus the Son of David with the very words Israel sang at the great feasts.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust in God. The withered fig tree becomes a lesson in believing prayer: faith that does not doubt lays hold of God's power, so that what seems immovable can be moved when His people ask according to His will.

basic.context: Jesus arranges to enter Jerusalem riding a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah's prophecy of the gentle King. Crowds spread cloaks and branches and shout Hosanna to the Son of David. He enters the temple, drives out the merchants, and calls it a house of prayer turned into a den of robbers. He heals the blind and lame there and accepts the children's praise, defending it from Scripture. The next morning He curses a leafy but fruitless fig tree, which withers, and teaches His disciples about believing prayer.
basic.hermeneutics: The entry is a deliberate, prophetic act: Jesus stages a royal arrival that says who He is, yet as a King of peace, not war. The temple cleansing and the fig tree belong together; both are enacted judgments on a religion that has the leaves of activity but no fruit for God. Read the crowd's Hosanna and the leaders' hostility side by side.
basic.originalLanguages: The King comes praus, gentle, on a donkey. The crowds cry Hosanna, save now, the ancient plea become praise. And Jesus teaches that pistis, faith without doubt, lays hold of God in prayer.
basic.typology: Jesus enters as the Davidic King of Zechariah 9 and cleanses the temple as its Lord, fulfilling Malachi's word that the Lord will suddenly come to His temple. The fig tree stands for fruitless Israel, an image the prophets used.
basic.christ: Jesus is the gentle King and Son of David, the Lord who comes to His temple to purify it, the one worthy of the praise of children and the healer of the broken. He is the true temple and the fruit God seeks.
basic.god: God comes to claim His house and will not tolerate its corruption. He ordains praise from the smallest and lowliest, and He judges leafy religion that bears no fruit. He answers the believing prayers of His people.
basic.crossReferences: Zechariah 9 foretells the gentle King on a donkey. Psalm 118 gives the Hosanna and blessed is He who comes. Isaiah 56 and Jeremiah 7 lie behind house of prayer and den of robbers. Psalm 8 grounds the children's praise.
basic.oneStory: The King foretold for centuries comes at last to His city, gentle and lowly, to shouts of salvation. He enters His temple as its Lord to purge it and to receive the praise of the least, and He pronounces judgment on fruitless religion. The story now stands at the gates of the passion: the welcomed King has come to His own place, and the week that leads to the cross has begun.

context.literary:
Matthew 21 is the hinge of the Gospel. Five great discourses have each ended with the same formula, 'when Jesus had finished,' and the narrative now turns from Galilee to the single week in Jerusalem that fills chapters 21 to 28. The geography is itself a sentence: Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, then the city, then the temple, then back to Bethany for the night, verses 1, 10, 12 and 17. Jesus moves in a tightening spiral toward the sanctuary, and everything in this section is staged in the temple's shadow.

The three scenes are woven as a sandwich. Verses 1 to 11 are a procession to the city, verses 12 to 17 a confrontation inside the sanctuary, and verses 18 to 22 a morning sign on the road back. The fig tree is not an afterthought; it is the interpretive frame placed around the temple action. Matthew tells the fig tree story in one block, where the other Gospel that records it splits it in two around the temple scene, so Matthew leaves it to the reader to connect them. What the tree shows in miniature, leaves with no fruit, the temple has just shown in full.

There is also a movement of acclamation and resistance. The crowds shout in verse 9, the whole city is shaken and asks a question in verse 10, the lame and blind come in verse 14, the children cry out in verse 15, and the leaders protest in verse 15. Each voice answers the question 'Who is this?' differently: a prophet from Nazareth, the Son of David, a healer, the one whose praise has been ordained. Only the leaders, who have the Scriptures, fail to answer rightly.

Finally, notice how the scene is built from quotation. The entry is introduced by a fulfilment formula, verses 4 and 5; the temple action by 'It is written,' verse 13; the children's praise by 'Have you never read,' verse 16. Jesus is not improvising a protest. Every act is interpreted by a text, and the question of who truly honors Scripture is already on the table, the very question the next two chapters will press.
context.historical:
Passover swelled Jerusalem many times beyond its ordinary size, and the pilgrims arrived from the Mount of Olives side, singing the psalms of ascent and the Hallel, Psalms 113 to 118. The royal imagery of the entry would have been understood at once. When Solomon was made king he rode David's own mule down to Gihon while the people shouted, 1 Kings 1:33-40, and when Jehu was proclaimed the men of his company laid their garments under him on the bare steps, 2 Kings 9:13. Cloaks on the road were the ancient way of spreading a carpet under a king. Branches were part of the festive vocabulary of the pilgrim feasts, and later Jewish writing connects waved branches with the rededication of the temple and with a conqueror's entry, which is one reason the crowd's enthusiasm could slide toward political hopes.

The donkey, however, carried a different message from the war horse. Kings who came to fight rode horses, and Zechariah 9:9 sets the donkey beside the removal of the chariot and the war bow, Zechariah 9:10. The Mount of Olives was also loaded with expectation. Zechariah 14:4 had the LORD's feet standing on that very mountain, east of Jerusalem, on the day He came to rescue His city. A Galilean teacher descending from that ridge with a crowd could not help but raise the memory.

The temple that Jesus entered was the vast Herodian complex, still under construction. Its outer court was open to Gentiles, and it was here that animals for sacrifice were sold and money changed, because the annual temple levy had to be paid in a particular silver coin rather than in common Roman or local currency. Doves were the offering of the poor, Leviticus 5:7 and Luke 2:24, so the sellers of doves were taking money from those with least. The system was lawful and convenient, and that is exactly the problem Jesus names: a place meant to draw the nations to prayer had become a place for commerce, and the commerce was controlled by the very priestly families who profited from it.

Fig trees in the region put out small early fruit before, or just as, the leaves unfold, so a tree in full leaf by the road announced that it ought to have something on it. That is why the sign works. A tree so dressed is making a claim it cannot honor.
context.canonical:
The entry is the only moment in the Gospels where Jesus openly accepts a royal reception, and Matthew links it with two Old Testament texts at once. The words 'Say to the Daughter of Zion' come from Isaiah 62:11, and the rest is Zechariah 9:9, so Matthew has woven together a word of salvation with a word of kingship. Zechariah 9 is a chapter about a king who brings peace to the nations and whose rule reaches 'from sea to sea,' Zechariah 9:10. Matthew has been building to this: 'Son of David' has been used by the blind and the Canaanite woman, and it reaches its fullest volume here, verse 9.

The crowd's words are from Psalm 118:25-26. This was the closing psalm of the Hallel, sung at Passover, and it is the psalm of the procession into the sanctuary gates. Its verses about the rejected stone, Psalm 118:22-23, are the very words Jesus will quote against the leaders a few verses on, Matthew 21:42, and its blessing on 'he who comes in the name of the LORD' will be quoted back at Jerusalem in Matthew 23:39. The psalm therefore opens and closes the whole controversy section.

The temple action combines Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. Isaiah promised that foreigners who joined themselves to the LORD would be brought to His holy mountain, and that His house would be a house of prayer for all the nations. Jeremiah stood at the temple gate and told the people that their trust in the building was a lie while they oppressed the stranger, the orphan and the widow, Jeremiah 7:4-11. Jesus holds the two together: the nations' access and the prophets' warning. Malachi 3:1 stands behind both, the Lord who suddenly comes to His temple.

The children's praise is Psalm 8:2, and the fig tree draws on the prophets' habit of describing Israel as a vine or fig tree that the LORD looked to for fruit, Hosea 9:10, Jeremiah 8:13 and Micah 7:1. In the New Testament the mountain saying is echoed in 1 Corinthians 13:2, and the promise about asking in prayer is developed in John 15:7 and 1 John 5:14.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wanted his readers, Jewish believers who had watched the temple leadership turn against Jesus, to see that the confrontation was not an accident of politics but the meeting of two kingdoms. He has set the entry in the language of Scripture so that no one can say Jesus slipped into messiahship by the back door. He comes openly, on the animal of the prophecy, to the shout of the pilgrim psalm, and He accepts it.

He also wanted them to see what kind of king this is. Zechariah's King is humble. The crowd wants a Son of David who will shake the empire, but the Son of David they get arrives in the way that undoes the idea of kingship as force, and then goes straight to a place of prayer and sets it right. For Matthew's church, which was living with the loss of the temple or the threat of it, the cleansing and the withered tree explained why the sanctuary was now under judgment and why the true house of prayer was gathering around Jesus.

The closing teaching on faith makes the point practical. After a judgment sign the disciples are told that they, too, have access to God's power, but through trusting prayer, not through a temple system. The author intends his readers to hear both warning and welcome.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Almost everything in this section is description of what only Jesus could do. No disciple is told to ride a donkey into a city and be hailed as king, and no church is commanded to overturn the tables of a bookshop in the lobby. The cleansing is the act of the Lord of the temple in His own house, and we should be careful about borrowing His authority for our own anger.

What is prescribed is quieter. The disciples are told, on the road, to trust God without doubt and to pray believing. The saying about the mountain is an instruction about faith, but it is not a blank cheque. It stands in the same Gospel that records Gethsemane, where Jesus asks and then submits, 'yet not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and in a letter that reminds us we ask 'according to His will,' 1 John 5:14. Prayer that trusts is not prayer that dictates. The scene also prescribes an examination of our own worship: a church can be full of leaves, activity, music and busyness, and still have nothing for God to eat.

debates.question: Why did Jesus curse the fig tree?

views.label: An enacted parable of fruitless Israel
views.case: The prophets spoke of Israel as a fig tree or vine from which God expected fruit, Hosea 9:10, Jeremiah 8:13, Micah 7:1, and Jesus had told a parable of a fig tree given one more year, Luke 13:6-9. Matthew frames the temple scene with the tree, so the withering reads as a verdict on a showy but barren system. The disciples ask about the tree, but the hostility of the leaders in the verses just before gives it its force.

views.label: A lesson in the power of trusting prayer
views.case: Matthew has Jesus answer the disciples' astonishment with a teaching on faith and prayer, verses 21 and 22, not with an explanation of Israel. On this view the miracle is a picture of what God does for those who ask without a divided mind, and the judgment overtones are a secondary reading imported from the context.

views.label: A sign of the time for fruit, with an unseasonable harvest in view
views.case: Another Gospel adds that it was not the season for figs, Mark 11:13, which has puzzled readers who ask why a tree should be cursed for lacking what it could not yet have. The usual answer is that early fruit comes with the leaves, so a tree in leaf promised something, and the point is the false promise, not the calendar. Matthew leaves the seasonal detail out entirely.

debates.bearing: The two main readings are not rivals. Matthew gives us a sign that judges leafy religion and then, in the same breath, uses its power to teach the disciples what a living, trusting faith looks like. Reading only the first makes the passage purely negative, and reading only the second loses the link to the temple.

debates.question: What was Jesus doing in the temple: reforming an abuse or announcing its end?

views.label: Reform: He was cleaning out corruption
views.case: His quotation of Jeremiah 7:11, 'a den of robbers,' points to oppression and fraud, and the Isaiah 56:7 line about prayer shows what the space was for. On this view He is acting as a prophet restoring right worship, which is why the blind and lame are healed there at once, verse 14.

views.label: Sign of judgment: He was enacting the temple's coming fall
views.case: A robber's den in Jeremiah 7 is not a place that is being repaired but one that is about to be destroyed, since the passage goes on to say it will go the way of Shiloh, Jeremiah 7:12-14. Jesus' later words, 'your house is left to you desolate,' Matthew 23:38, and His prediction that not one stone will remain, Matthew 24:2, fit this reading, as does the fig tree beside it.

views.label: Claim of the Lord to His own house
views.case: The cleansing is first of all an assertion of authority, which is why the leaders at once ask 'by what authority' in Matthew 21:23. The acts do not rest on a technical complaint about prices but on the fact that the Lord of the house has come, as Malachi 3:1 said.

debates.bearing: The first and third readings are not far apart, and the second is the natural completion of both. Jesus purges because He is Lord, and He purges as a sign that a system which will not receive its Lord is already under the sentence of Jeremiah.

study.originalLanguages:
The word praus in verse 5 is the key to how Matthew reads Zechariah. Matthew uses praus once more in the Gospel, when Jesus says 'I am gentle and humble in heart,' Matthew 11:29, and once in the Beatitudes in its plural form, 'Blessed are the meek,' Matthew 5:5. The BSB of Zechariah 9:9 reads 'humble,' and the Greek Old Testament uses the same word Matthew does. So Matthew's King is the same person who invited the weary to find rest in His gentleness. The quotation is not a decorative proof text; it is a description of His character. The word does not mean weak. It names strength that is under control and placed at the service of others.

The 'donkey' and the 'colt' have bothered readers because the Hebrew of Zechariah 9:9 is a parallelism, 'on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey,' one animal described twice. Matthew alone has the disciples fetch both animals, a donkey with her colt beside her, verses 2 and 7. Some take this as Matthew reading the line literally, and some as a way of saying that the unbroken colt is accompanied by its mother to keep it calm. Either way he has not misread the poetry; he has seen that the prophecy names a mount that has never been ridden, which is the kind of animal reserved for a king in Scripture.

The word 'Hosanna' is the Hebrew hoshi'a na, 'save, we pray,' from Psalm 118:25, where it is a cry addressed to the LORD. By Jesus' day it had become a shout of acclamation, so the crowd is part pleading and part praising. Matthew gives it a dative, 'Hosanna to the Son of David,' which turns the plea into an address to the king. The cry 'Hosanna in the highest' calls on the highest heaven to confirm the salvation requested.

When Jesus enters the city, the whole city 'was stirred,' verse 10. The verb is the one for shaking, from the same family as the Greek word for an earthquake, and Matthew uses it of the earth's quaking at the cross and the guards trembling at the tomb, Matthew 27:51 and 28:2 to 4. It is a strong choice: Jerusalem's first reaction is a tremor.

The 'robbers' of verse 13 are lestai, a word that means bandits or violent brigands, not petty thieves. A den of lestai is where bandits retreat to after raiding. The picture is not that the money changers stole at the tables but that the temple had become the hideout where they felt safe. It is the word that appears again at His arrest, when He asks whether they have come out with swords and clubs to arrest Him as they would an outlaw, Matthew 26:55, where the Greek word is the same lestes. The one who calls the temple a robbers' den is treated as a robber in the same city.

Finally, the word translated 'do not doubt' in verse 21 comes from diakrino, which means to separate or to discriminate and so to be divided in mind. It is the word in James 1:6, 'without doubting,' and the image is of a person pulled in two directions. The opposite of faith here is not an honest question but a split loyalty. And the verb for 'ordained' in the quotation of Psalm 8:2 is katartizo in the Greek Old Testament, a word for putting something in good order, so that the children's praise has been equipped and made ready by God and not simply allowed.

typology.type: The humble King of Zechariah 9 and the kings who came before him
typology.fulfillment: Solomon rode a royal mule to his anointing, 1 Kings 1:33-40, and Jehu was hailed on a carpet of cloaks, 2 Kings 9:13. Jesus reproduces the scene but changes its meaning. Where earlier kings were proclaimed with trumpets and left behind a cost in blood, this Son of David arrives to give His own life, as He has told the disciples three times in Matthew 16 to 20. Zechariah 9:10 promises that this King will speak peace to the nations, and the same Gospel ends with Him sending the disciples to all nations, Matthew 28:19. The type falls short in that earlier kings were crowned by their friends; this King is crowned by mockers a week later, Matthew 27:29.

typology.type: The Lord who comes suddenly to His temple, Malachi 3:1
typology.fulfillment: Malachi had promised a messenger to prepare the way and then the Lord Himself arriving at His temple. Matthew has already identified John as the messenger, Matthew 11:10, so the arrival of the Lord must follow. The Lord who comes is also the Messenger of the covenant, and Malachi goes on to say He will refine and purify, Malachi 3:2-3. Jesus does exactly that in the courts. In John's Gospel He then speaks of the temple of His body, John 2:19-21, and the New Testament says that believers are the living temple, 1 Peter 2:5 and Ephesians 2:21. The type is exceeded because the building that was cleansed is itself replaced by the One who was always its meaning.

typology.type: The barren fig tree and the planted vine
typology.fulfillment: The prophets speak of Israel as God's planting that was expected to yield, Isaiah 5:1-7, Hosea 9:10. The tree in leaf without fruit stands for a nation and a sanctuary with every outward sign of life and nothing for God. Jesus' words that it will never bear again, verse 19, look forward to the parable of the tenants in the next study, where the kingdom is taken from fruitless stewards. Yet the type carries hope as well as warning, because the Gospel's way of dealing with barrenness is to graft and to give a Fruit-bearing Vine, John 15:1-5. Israel the tree could not bear what Israel the vine was meant to bear, and Jesus, who calls Himself the true vine, does.

typology.type: The praise ordained from infants, Psalm 8:2
typology.fulfillment: In Psalm 8 the praise of children silences the enemy and avenger, and the psalm turns at once to humanity's dignity, Psalm 8:4-6. Jesus applies the psalm to the children crying to the Son of David and so identifies Himself with the LORD to whom the psalm is addressed. Hebrews 2:5-9 then reads the rest of Psalm 8 of Jesus, the human being crowned with glory and honor through suffering. The correspondence is that the weakest voices are the ones God uses to confound the strong. The type is exceeded because the children praise a King whom the learned refuse.

study.christ:
This chapter shows Jesus acting in three roles at once, and the Old Testament has prepared each of them. He is the King of Zechariah 9, who comes with salvation in His hand and not a sword. He is the Lord of Malachi 3, who arrives at His temple to refine it. And He is the Son of David of the Hallel, the one the pilgrims greet with the psalm that says 'blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD.' It is striking that Jesus lets all three go unchallenged. He does not rebuke the crowd; later He tells the objecting Pharisees that the stones would cry out if the disciples fell silent, Luke 19:40. The silence of Jesus in the face of royal acclaim is part of the Gospel's argument that He is who they say He is.

The gentleness of the King matters for how we think of His power. Matthew has already shown the powerful Jesus, who calms the sea and raises the dead, and he now shows the same Jesus riding a borrowed animal. Paul will say that Christ Jesus 'made Himself nothing,' Philippians 2:7, and that is the path by which He is exalted. The King does not become gentle in order to reach the cross; He is gentle, and the cross is the form His kingship takes.

The temple action is a Christological claim, not only a moral one. To drive out the sellers from God's house with a word of Scripture is to speak and act as one with authority over that house. In John the claim is explicit: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,' John 2:19. The New Testament builds on this. In Christ the glory that filled the temple dwells in a body, John 1:14, and through Him the nations have access to the Father, Ephesians 2:18, which is what Isaiah 56:7 promised when it said the house would be for all peoples. The blind and the lame, who were barred from the inner priestly service by the law, Leviticus 21:18, come to Him in the temple and are healed. He does not clear the temple of the weak but of those who prey on them.

Jesus also stands as the one who bears the fruit God seeks. The fig tree is the failure of a nation, but the tree is not the last word. The Gospels present the faithful servant, the true Israel who obeys the Father in the wilderness and in the garden. Against the leaves of religious display, He is the Man whose whole life is for the Father's table.

We should keep a guard against over-reading. The donkey is not a code for any one doctrine, and the withered tree is not a puzzle for every botanist. The links are those the Gospel makes itself, by formula quotation and by the structure of the week, and they all point to one conclusion: the King has come to His house, and He does not come as the crowd expected.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is that He keeps promises at the level of detail. The location of the entry, the animal, the cry of the crowd, and the quarrel in the temple all rest on words God spoke centuries before. Zechariah's prophecy and Malachi's warning are not general moods but exact commitments. When Jesus sends the disciples to a village where the animals will be found, He shows the same command over circumstance that God shows over history, and verse 3 gives His own title for it, 'the Lord needs them.' The One who possesses all things asks for a borrowed donkey, and the owner lets it go.

The passage also shows a God who cares about the place and manner of worship. The temple is 'My house,' verse 13, and His anger is not at religion but at what stands in the way of prayer. Isaiah had said that God's house would be for the nations, and the court where the traders worked was the one part of the temple that foreigners could enter. A God who cares about the outsider's room to pray is a God whose zeal is for the least, and the surprise of verse 14 is that the first people who come into the cleansed space are the blind and the lame.

God is shown as the one who ordains praise. Verse 16 quotes the psalm to say that it is God Himself who equips the children to praise. The praise of the weak is not an accident of enthusiasm but a work of God, and it is the answer to the claim of the strong. We worship a God who does not need the endorsement of the learned.

Here, as elsewhere, judgment and mercy are held together. The sign of the tree is severe, and the healing of the sick in the temple is tender, and both come from the same Lord in the same hours. The tension is not resolved by softening either. A God who is truly good must care that His house is used to exploit the poor, and a God who is truly good heals the broken in that same house on the same day.

For worship, the passage asks whether we come with leaves or fruit. It asks whether our gatherings make room for the outsider and the weak, whether we welcome God's praise from unlikely mouths, and whether we pray believing. The right response to a God who enters His house is neither to hide in the activity nor to panic at the cleansing, but to receive the King who comes in gentleness and to lay down our cloaks.

crossReferences.note: The prophecy Matthew quotes, joined to Isaiah 62:11. The King is righteous and victorious, yet humble, and the line after it speaks of cutting off the chariot and the war bow and of peace to the nations. Matthew's choice of the gentle word shows he reads the entry as a disclosure of character, not just a staged fulfilment.

The Hallel's closing psalm, sung at Passover, is the source of 'Hosanna' and 'blessed is he who comes.' Its next verses speak of the rejected stone and the procession to the altar, which is why the whole controversy section of Matthew can be read as a single unfolding of this psalm.

Solomon was set on David's mule and brought down to Gihon to the sound of the trumpet and the shouts of the people. The echo is deliberate: a Son of David is publicly acclaimed on a royal animal, and the earth rings with the noise. Jesus' entry is the greater Solomon's, but He is hailed in a week that will end in a cross.

When Jehu was proclaimed, each man took his garment and put it under him on the steps. The cloaks of Matthew 21:8 belong to the same gesture of homage. The contrast is that Jehu's reign came through bloodshed, and the crowd in Jerusalem hopes for a Jehu while receiving a Shepherd.

The house of prayer for all the nations. Matthew leaves out the words 'for all the nations,' but the Isaiah context speaks of foreigners and eunuchs welcomed to God's mountain. The traders in the court of the Gentiles had crowded out the very people for whom the verse was written.

The den of robbers line comes from Jeremiah's temple sermon, in which the people trusted in the building while they oppressed the vulnerable. The verse goes on to warn that God will do to this house what He did to Shiloh, so the cleansing carries a warning of destruction as well as reform.

After the messenger who prepares the way, the Lord suddenly comes to His temple. Matthew has already applied the messenger to John, Matthew 11:10, so the next line is the Lord's own arrival. Malachi goes on to describe a refining fire, which is what the temple courts experience.

The children's praise, ordained by God, is the weapon against the 'enemy and avenger.' Jesus uses the line to answer the indignant priests, turning the psalm of human dignity into a defense of Himself. The psalm says God establishes strength from the weakest mouths.

God says He found Israel like grapes in the wilderness and saw the fathers as the firstfruits of the fig tree. The fig tree is the image of God's early delight in His people and of His disappointment. Jesus' tree in leaf by the road gathers up this long history of expected fruit.

The LORD says there will be no grapes on the vine nor figs on the tree, and even the leaf will wither. The prophecy of a barren nation under judgment is exactly the picture of the tree in Matthew 21:19, which withers at once.

Luke's account of the same approach adds that Jesus wept over the city and said the stones would cry out if the disciples were silent. The tears at the gate show the heart behind the cleansing: the King enters in sorrow because Jerusalem did not recognize the time of her visitation.

Paul takes up the mountain-moving image and says that faith able to remove mountains is nothing without love. It is a needed companion to Matthew 21:21, which can sound like a promise of power, because it keeps believing prayer from becoming a means of getting our own way.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning God intended to dwell with His people. In Eden He walked in the garden, Genesis 3:8, and the tabernacle and temple were His provision for living among a people who had been sent east of the garden. Every part of the temple, its courts and its veil, was a sign of both access and distance. By Jesus' day that sign had become a source of profit and a barrier to the nations, and the work of this chapter is to bring the temple story to a point of decision.

The prophets had long said what would come. Zechariah had seen a King on a donkey, Malachi a Lord who comes suddenly, Isaiah a house for all nations and Jeremiah a house under threat. Daniel and the Psalms add the Son of David who is more than David's son. The entry gathers those threads: the King arrives, and the pilgrim psalm is sung to Him, and for a moment it seems as if Israel's long waiting has been answered.

But it is also the hour of division. The same city that is shaken asks 'Who is this?', and the answer comes in different shapes. The children and the blind receive Him, and the leaders resist, and the tree withers. The story of Israel as God's vine, with its long record of promised fruit and disappointment, is brought to a climax. In the next study, the parable of the tenants will say the same thing in a story, and in Matthew 23 the same house will be called 'your house.'

The story is not left in judgment. The King who enters is already walking toward the cross, where He will be both temple and sacrifice, both King and the one handed over. At His death the veil is torn from top to bottom, Matthew 27:51, and the sanctuary is no longer a place the nations stand outside of. The disciples who watched the fig tree wither will be sent to make disciples of every nation, and the house of prayer for all peoples will be filled.

The new creation completes the picture. John sees no temple in the New Jerusalem, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22, and the nations walk by its light, Revelation 21:24. The King who rode into Jerusalem on a borrowed donkey will be acclaimed by 'a great multitude from every nation,' Revelation 7:9, and the praise that the children began will be the praise of the whole creation. The shouts of Hosanna, save now, will be answered at last when He wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: What does the manner of Jesus' entry reveal about His kingship?

options.text: He comes as the gentle King of Zechariah's prophecy, humble on a donkey rather than a warhorse.
options.note: Verses 4-5 present Jesus fulfilling Zechariah 9:9 as the gentle King.

options.text: He comes as a royal figure welcomed by the crowds.
options.note: True, but it omits the deliberate humility, the donkey and Zechariah's gentle King, that defines His reign.

options.text: He comes as a military leader to overthrow Rome.
options.note: The donkey signals peace, not military conquest; He deliberately avoids that image.

options.text: He enters secretly to avoid drawing attention.
options.note: The entry is public and staged to fulfill prophecy, the opposite of secret.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus cleanse the temple?

options.text: Because His house of prayer had been turned into a den of robbers, and He came as its Lord to purify it.
options.note: Verses 12-13 show Jesus reclaiming the temple's true purpose from corruption.

options.text: Because He objected to any buying and selling near the temple.
options.note: The issue was corruption of the house of prayer, not commerce as such; this misses the deeper indictment.

options.text: Because the priests had asked Him to reform the temple.
options.note: The leaders were indignant, not requesting reform; Jesus acted on His own authority.

options.text: Because the temple was to be abandoned entirely.
options.note: He purifies it as a house of prayer rather than abandoning it here.

quiz.q: What did the cursing of the barren fig tree signify?

options.text: A judgment on fruitless religion that has leaves of show but no fruit for God.
options.note: The leafy but fruitless tree pictures barren religion, framing the temple scene.

options.text: A lesson about the power of believing prayer.
options.note: Jesus does draw that lesson, but the sign itself first pronounces judgment on fruitlessness.

options.text: Jesus' frustration that He was hungry.
options.note: His hunger is the occasion, but the act is a deliberate enacted parable, not mere frustration.

options.text: A promise that all trees would obey Him.
options.note: The point is fruitfulness and faith, not power over trees in general.

quiz.q: How did Jesus respond to the children shouting Hosanna in the temple?

options.text: He accepted their praise and defended it from Psalm 8, that God ordains praise from children.
options.note: Verse 16 shows Jesus welcoming the children's worship as fitting Scripture.

options.text: He told the children to be quieter so as not to offend the leaders.
options.note: The opposite; He affirmed their praise rather than silencing it.

options.text: He ignored the children and focused on the adults.
options.note: He specifically drew attention to and defended the children's praise.

options.text: He agreed with the leaders that the praise was inappropriate.
options.note: He affirmed the children against the leaders' indignation.

questions: The King came gentle and lowly, not on a warhorse. How does the humility of Jesus' kingship challenge your ideas of power and greatness?
The crowds cried Hosanna, save now. What do you most need Jesus to save you from, and are you crying out to Him for it?
Jesus cleansed His house of what did not belong. What might He want to drive out of your own worship and heart to make room for prayer?
The fig tree had leaves but no fruit. Where might your life have the appearance of faith without the fruit God is looking for?
Jesus welcomed the praise of children. Where do you need to come to God with childlike, unguarded worship rather than adult self-consciousness?

translationNotes.note: The quotation is Zechariah 9:9; Matthew mentions both the donkey and the colt, and the crowd lays cloaks on them, highlighting the fulfillment rather than implying Jesus rode both at once.
Hosanna transliterates the Hebrew of Psalm 118:25, save now or save, we pray, which had become a shout of praise; the whole acclamation draws on Psalm 118:25-26.
Jesus joins two prophetic texts, my house will be called a house of prayer from Isaiah 56:7 and a den of robbers from Jeremiah 7:11, to indict the temple's corruption.
